analysis.one_liner: Slashes taxes on estates, corporations, and investment gains while offering a simplified three-bracket income tax.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on January 6, 2009 and received no further action, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the tax code in two directions at once. It offered a simpler optional income tax with three rates, made a fix to the alternative minimum tax permanent, let people without employer health coverage deduct more medical expenses, and created new tax-free savings accounts. But its biggest provisions cut taxes on concentrated wealth: it repealed the estate and gift tax entirely, cut the top corporate rate from 35% to 25%, cut the capital gains rate from 15% to 10%, let investors adjust the value of assets for inflation before calculating taxable gains, made the research tax credit permanent, and made the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts permanent. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and died there without a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the largest dollar benefits would have gone to the wealthiest households: heirs of large estates (the estate tax applies only to the biggest inheritances), investors with large capital gains (a 10% top rate plus inflation indexing reduces their tax), and profitable corporations (a 25% top rate instead of 35%). Middle-income taxpayers would have gained more modestly, mainly from the permanent AMT fix, the optional simplified three-bracket tax, the expanded medical-expense deduction for people without employer coverage, and the new tax-advantaged savings and job-training accounts.

how_it_helps.text: It lets people without employer health coverage and under 65 deduct medical expenses without meeting the normal income threshold, up to $7,500 per person or $15,000 per family [S2][S3].

It makes the higher alternative minimum tax (AMT) exemption amounts permanent and adjusts them for inflation, sparing more middle-income households from a parallel tax originally aimed at the wealthy [S2].

It creates new tax-advantaged Retirement Savings Accounts, Lifetime Savings Accounts, and Lifetime Skills Accounts (up to $5,000, $5,000, and $1,000 per year respectively), with tax-free withdrawals for retirement, general savings, and job-training expenses [S2][S3].
It offers an optional simplified income tax with three brackets (10%, 15%, 30%) that taxpayers could choose instead of the regular system [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury — and ultimately taxpayers or recipients of federal programs — would bear the cost of the lost revenue from estate tax repeal, the corporate and capital gains cuts, inflation indexing, and making the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts permanent. Within the tax code, households that rely on deductions and credits the simplified system omits could pay more if they elected it, and repeal of the estate tax removes a progressive levy that falls exclusively on very large inheritances.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the estate and gift tax outright, cutting the top corporate rate from 35% to 25%, dropping the capital gains rate to 10%, and indexing asset values for inflation concentrate their benefits on large estates, high-income investors, and profitable corporations, while reducing federal revenue that funds public services [S2][S3].

The bill makes the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts (the 'Bush tax cuts') permanent by repealing their expiration dates, locking in lower top rates rather than letting Congress reconsider them each decade [S3].

The simplified alternative system allows only a few deductions (personal exemptions, home-mortgage interest, state and local income taxes, charitable gifts, and limited medical expenses) and keeps only the child tax credit, so taxpayers electing it would give up many existing credits and deductions [S3].
Adding an elective parallel tax system with inflation-indexed asset basis would add record-keeping and compliance complexity, cutting against the bill's 'simple' framing [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill bundled genuinely useful ideas — a simpler three-bracket rate structure, a permanent AMT fix, easier medical-expense deductions for people without employer coverage, and new savings accounts — with provisions whose benefits flow overwhelmingly upward: full estate tax repeal, a lower capital gains rate, inflation indexing of investment gains, and a corporate rate cut, all with no stated way to replace the lost revenue. The worthwhile simplification pieces were inseparable from the large tax cuts on inherited and investment wealth, and the bill died without a hearing or an official cost estimate, so its true fiscal price was never established.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the House tax-writing committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no vote, and no further action for the rest of the two-year Congress.

narrative.text: The bill's entire recorded history is two actions on January 6, 2009: introduction and referral to the Ways and Means Committee [S5].
It never attracted support beyond its sponsor and three Republican cosponsors [S4].

Its major provisions — estate tax repeal, a 25% corporate rate, a 10% capital gains rate, and permanent extension of the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts — were the opposite of the tax policy the new Democratic majority and incoming Obama administration pursued in 2009 [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody gained or lost money, since the bill never advanced; the practical effect was to preserve the existing tax code, including the estate tax and the 35% corporate rate.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the tax code stayed as it was

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes to measure, but all four sponsors were Republicans and the Democratic-controlled Ways and Means Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: Full repeal of the estate and gift tax would eliminate tax on inherited wealth entirely, a benefit available only to the largest estates. Combined with the lower capital gains rate and inflation indexing of asset values, the bill's largest-dollar benefits flow to the wealthiest families.

Cutting the top corporate rate from 35% to 25% is a broad tax reduction for profitable companies. The public cost is forgone revenue; the benefit to companies does not depend on any commitment to wages or prices.

New Retirement, Lifetime Savings, and Lifetime Skills Accounts must be held through banks or approved trustees, creating new tax-advantaged account business for the financial industry. Savers who use the accounts benefit too, so the industry's gain runs alongside theirs, though fees would skim some of the tax advantage.

Making the research and experimentation credit permanent converts a recurring lobbying fight into a guaranteed subsidy. It supports R&D jobs, but it is a permanent tax benefit for a concentrated set of large firms.
